FLINT: Fixed-budget Late Interaction

Himank Handa Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign    Negar Arabzadeh Affiliation: University of California, Berkeleyhimankh2@illinois.edu, {negara, matei}@berkeley.edu    Matei Zaharia Affiliation: University of California, Berkeleyhimankh2@illinois.edu, {negara, matei}@berkeley.edu
Abstract

Multi-vector retrieval models such as ColBERT often outperform single-vector models of comparable scale by matching queries and documents at the token level. However, retaining a vector for every token substantially increases storage requirements and slows retrieval compared to single-vector bi-encoders, limiting their scalability. We introduce FLINT (Fixed-budget Late INTeraction), an architecture that uses attention-based pooling to represent each query and document with a fixed number of embedding vectors. Unlike architectures that pool only document representations while retaining token-level queries, FLINT applies pooling symmetrically to both sides, limiting document storage and the number of vector comparisons needed during retrieval. FLINT achieves comparable ranking effectiveness to the closest baselines on BEIR and outperforms them on several benchmarks with longer and more complex queries, including BrowseComp+, CRUMB, and TREC Tip-of-the-Tongue 2025. We demonstrate that FLINT’s effectiveness–efficiency benefits extend across encoder architectures, testing it on two separate backbones (BERT and ModernBERT). On long-query corpora, FLINT delivers 1.5–2.8× faster end-to-end retrieval than ConstBERT, the closest baseline. FLINT also reduces index size by 5.3–9.3× relative to token-level late-interaction models such as ColBERTv2.

1 Introduction

Multi-vector retrieval models such as ColBERT often outperform bi-encoders (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) of comparable scale because they preserve token-level representations and enable fine-grained matching between query and document tokens (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020). However, this effectiveness comes at a substantial cost in latency and storage. While a standard bi-encoder stores a single vector for each document, ColBERT-style models store one vector for every document token. Consequently, their index size grows with document length, substantially increasing storage requirements and retrieval-time computation, which leads to higher latency and limits scalability.

ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al., 2022b) substantially reduces ColBERT’s storage footprint through residual compression and improves retrieval effectiveness while retaining token-level representations. The PLAID index (Santhanam et al., 2022a; MacAvaney and Tonellotto, 2024) further improves retrieval efficiency through centroid-based candidate filtering and pruning. XTR (Lee et al., 2023) scores documents using retrieved tokens and estimates missing token similarities. WARP (Scheerer et al., 2025) accelerates XTR-style retrieval by computing scores directly from compressed token embeddings. MUVERA (Dhulipala et al., 2024) uses fixed-dimensional encodings for single-vector MIPS search, followed by multi-vector reranking. Despite these advances, storage requirements remain large and tied to document length through token-level representations retained for ranking.

MacAvaney et al. (2025) address these efficiency limitations by proposing ConstBERT, in which they pool each document into a fixed set of 32 embedding vectors. This fixed representation substantially reduces index sizes relative to ColBERTv2 while preserving effectiveness on MS MARCO and BEIR. However, ConstBERT retains one embedding vector per query token, so the number of query vectors and the associated search cost still grow with longer and more complex queries, where latency also increases. This motivates the question: Can we design a fixed-budget late-interaction architecture that preserves effectiveness on long, complex, out-of-distribution queries while reducing both document storage and query-side search cost? We give a more detailed comparison with related work in Appendix A.

To retain the storage efficiency of fixed-budget representations without sacrificing effectiveness, and to further reduce retrieval latency, we introduce FLINT (Fixed-budget Late INTeraction). The key idea is to retain multiple representations for matching without tying each representation to a single input token. As illustrated in Figure 1, learned latent vectors attend over the full token sequence, each aggregating information from multiple tokens into an output embedding. Thus, longer inputs can change the information captured by these embeddings without increasing their number. The pooling module converts each variable-length token sequence into a fixed number of embedding vectors for multi-vector retrieval and replaces the single-vector mean-pooling operation commonly used in bi-encoders. Figure 2 compares FLINT’s architecture with prior models. Unlike ConstBERT, FLINT applies attention-based pooling symmetrically to both documents and queries. As a result, FLINT’s storage cost per document is independent of document length, and its fixed query-vector budget keeps late-interaction search latency nearly constant as query length increases.

We evaluate FLINT on standard general-domain retrieval benchmarks, as well as out-of-domain benchmarks featuring substantially longer and more complex queries. On BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021), FLINT outperforms the single-vector baseline and remains competitive with existing late-interaction models, while requiring substantially less storage than token-level retrieval. On more complex benchmarks, including CRUMB (Killingback and Zamani, 2025), TREC Tip-of-the-Tongue 2025 (Arguello et al., 2026), and BrowseComp+ (Chen et al., 2026), FLINT generally provides stronger retrieval effectiveness than ConstBERT. These results show that FLINT fixed-budget representations on both the query and document sides can retain strong retrieval effectiveness even for long, out-of-distribution queries.

FLINT combines these effectiveness results with substantial savings in storage and retrieval time. FLINT reduces index size by 5.35.3–9.3×9.3\times relative to token-level late-interaction models. Beyond reducing storage, FLINT substantially improves retrieval-time efficiency. Because it produces a fixed number of vectors for both documents and queries, its search cost remains nearly constant as query length increases. On the evaluated long-query corpora, FLINT achieves 1.5–2.8×\times faster end-to-end retrieval and 2.52.5–4.8×4.8\times faster search time than ConstBERT. We note that FLINT is orthogonal to other existing efficiency techniques, including dimensionality reduction and PLAID indexing (Santhanam et al., 2022a), which can provide complementary improvements in storage and retrieval speed. We evaluate FLINT with ModernBERT-large (Warner et al., 2025) as an alternative backbone and show that its effectiveness–efficiency benefits remain robust.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce FLINT11 1 Our code is available at https://github.com/hmk55555/FLINT, and model checkpoints at https://huggingface.co/collections/himankhanda/flint. , a fixed-budget late-interaction architecture that applies symmetric attention-based pooling to both document and query representations, decoupling storage and retrieval cost from input length.

  • •

    We show that FLINT outperforms a single-vector baseline, remains competitive with existing late-interaction models on standard benchmarks and better preserves effectiveness on longer, out-of-distribution queries, while achieving lower retrieval latency than ConstBERT.

  • •

    We demonstrate that FLINT generalizes across backbones and exposes the vector budget VV as a tunable effectiveness–efficiency trade-off.

2 FLINT: Fixed-Budget Late Interaction

2.1 Fixed-Budget Representations

Given a query qq and a document dd, a shared transformer backbone (Vaswani et al., 2017) independently encodes each input into a sequence of contextualized, hh-dimensional representations. Let Xq∈ℝ|q|×hX_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{|q|\times h} and Xd∈ℝ|d|×hX_{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{|d|\times h} denote the resulting query and document representations, respectively, where |q||q| and |d||d| are the numbers of query and document tokens, and hh is the hidden dimensionality of the transformer.

In standard late-interaction models such as ColBERT, all token representations are retained for scoring. Consequently, the number of stored document vectors grows with document length, while the cost of query–document matching grows with the number of query and document vectors. To address this limitation, FLINT inserts an attention-based pooling module between the transformer and the late-interaction scoring layer. The module maps the variable-length query and document representations, XqX_{q} and XdX_{d}, to fixed-budget pooled representations Zq,Zd∈ℝV×hZ_{q},Z_{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times h}, where VV denotes the fixed number of vectors allocated to each query and document. Thus, FLINT stores exactly VV vectors per document or query, regardless of document length |d||d| or query length |q||q|.

2.2 Symmetric Attention-Based Pooling

FLINT builds on the cross-attention pooling mechanism used in the Perceiver Resampler architecture (Alayrac et al., 2022; Jaegle et al., 2021), which we adapt to fixed-budget late-interaction retrieval. For each input side s∈{q,d}s\in\{q,d\}, a fixed set of VV learned latent vectors Ls∈ℝV×hL_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times h} attends over the corresponding backbone representations XsX_{s}. The latent vectors act as attention queries, while the token representations act as keys and values. This operation summarizes the full variable-length token sequence into exactly VV output vectors.

For an input representation X∈ℝn×hX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times h}, where n∈{|q|,|d|}n\in\{|q|,|d|\} and learned latents L∈ℝV×hL\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times h}, the pooling operation is

Pool⁡(L,X)=softmax⁡((L​WQ)​(X​WK)⊤ha)​X​WV,\mathrm{Pool}(L,X)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{(LW_{Q})(XW_{K})^{\top}}{\sqrt{h_{a}}}\right)XW_{V}, (1)

where WQW_{Q}, WKW_{K}, and WVW_{V} are learned projection matrices, and ha=h/Hh_{a}=h/H is the per-head dimensionality for HH attention heads. The module uses multi-head attention followed by an output projection. Its output contains exactly VV vectors in ℝV×h\mathbb{R}^{V\times h}, regardless of the input length nn.

Each cross-attention output is then refined by a position-wise feed-forward network applied identically and independently to each of the VV latent vectors. The feed-forward network consists of an up-projection from hh to r​hrh dimensions, a GELU nonlinearity, and a down-projection from r​hrh back to hh. Figure 1 illustrates our pooling module 22 2 We experimented with modules containing various depth self-attention stacks, but found those to lead to complete document vectors and score collapse, documented in the Appendix D.. The number of heads, the ratio rr, and the projection dimension are given in Appendix B.

Document and query encoders share the same transformer backbone, pooling module, and linear projection parameters. Only the learned latent sets, LqL_{q} and LdL_{d}, are specific to the query and document sides, respectively. After pooling, the resulting representations Zq,ZdZ_{q},Z_{d} are projected into the retrieval embedding space and scored using ColBERT’s standard late-interaction operator. Let ziqz_{i}^{q} and zjdz_{j}^{d} denote the ii-th and jj-th rows of the projected ZqZ_{q} and ZdZ_{d}, i.e. the ii-th projected query vector and the jj-th projected document vector, respectively. FLINT computes

S⁡(q,d)=∑i=1Vmaxj∈{1,…,V}⁡(ziq)⊤​zjd.S(q,d)=\sum_{i=1}^{V}\max_{j\in\{1,\ldots,V\}}\left(z_{i}^{q}\right)^{\top}z_{j}^{d}. (2)

This is the same MaxSim scoring function used by ColBERTv2 and ConstBERT, but it is computed over exactly VV query and VV document vectors rather than over a variable number of token-level representations. Figure 2 shows FLINT architecture relative to baselines:

  • •

    (a) ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020) retains one vector for every query and document token. The resulting token-level representations are projected and compared using MaxSim. Consequently, the document index grows with document length, and matching cost increases with the numbers of query and document tokens.

  • •

    (b) ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al., 2022b) uses the same token-level late-interaction architecture but applies dimensionality reduction to reduce the storage cost of its index. However, it still retains one representation per token, so index size and matching cost remain dependent on document and query length.

  • •

    (c) ConstBERT reduces the document-side cost by pooling each document into a fixed set of VV vectors (V=32V=32), but it retains one representation per query token, so retrieval cost can still increase for longer queries.

  • •

    (d) FLINT applies the shared cross-attention and FFN pooling module to both queries and documents. The pooling parameters are shared, while the query and document latent vectors are learned separately. FLINT therefore produces exactly VV vectors on both sides, keeping the index size fixed per document and limiting the number of query vectors used during late-interaction scoring.

3 Experiments

3.1 Datasets

We evaluate FLINT across four complementary retrieval suites spanning diverse tasks, queries, and corpus sizes. BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021) represents conventional zero-shot retrieval across heterogeneous domains, including question answering, fact verification, and biomedical search, with predominantly short and keyword-like queries. CRUMB (Killingback and Zamani, 2025), in contrast, covers multi-aspect and reasoning-intensive retrieval tasks whose queries express multiple constraints, use domain-specific terminology, and often have limited lexical overlap with relevant documents.

We additionally evaluate two retrieval settings that differ substantially from standard passage retrieval. TREC Tip-of-the-Tongue 2025 (Arguello et al., 2026) evaluates known-item re-finding from long, conversational descriptions that may include vague details, comparisons, and incorrect recollections. BrowseComp+ (Chen et al., 2026) evaluates deep-research retrieval, where systems must identify human-verified supporting evidence among challenging distractor documents. Together, these suites cover both short, conventional information needs and longer, out-of-distribution queries. This long and complex query regime is particularly important for evaluating FLINT because the retrieval cost of token-level late-interaction models grows with the number of query representations. Details of dataset statistics are reported in Appendix C.

3.2 Baselines

Our primary goal is to isolate the effectiveness and efficiency trade-offs introduced by the retrieval architecture, rather than compare independently optimized retrieval systems. We therefore focus on controlled comparisons with single-vector, token-level late-interaction, and document-only fixed-budget architectures, using matched backbones and training settings where possible. Methods such as XTR (Lee et al., 2023; Scheerer et al., 2025), token pruning (Acquavia et al., 2023), and other indexing or compression techniques address related efficiency challenges but modify different components of the retrieval pipeline. We discuss these approaches in Appendix A. Here, we compare the results of our FLINT BERT model against ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al., 2022b) and ConstBERT (MacAvaney et al., 2025). On ModernBERT, we compare against ColBERTv2, ConstBERT, and single-vector-based architectures.

3.3 Training Setup & Implementation

Training. We train FLINT on the same MS MARCO (Bajaj et al., 2016) training set used in ColBERTv2 (Santhanam et al., 2022b) and ConstBERT (MacAvaney et al., 2025) so that any effectiveness gap between the three models reflects the pooling architecture rather than a difference in training data. We evaluate the trained models for ColBERT and ConstBERT on our exact setup to ensure fair comparison. In testing an alternate backbone, we replace BERT with ModernBERT while keeping FLINT’s symmetric attention-based pooling architecture unchanged. Since the exact multi-vector ModernBERT checkpoint used in prior work is not publicly available, we train the ColBERTv2 architecture on ModernBERT using the same training regimen as in Warner et al. (2025). We train FLINT under the same setup, enabling a controlled comparison between token-level and fixed-budget late interaction. We additionally train ConstBERT on ModernBERT under the same regimen, and train FLINT with budgets V∈{16,32,64}V\in\{16,32,64\}; unless noted, FLINT results use V=32V{=}32. As a single-vector baseline, we use an existing ModernBERT-large bi-encoder. Additional training, sequence lengths, query padding, and indexing details are described in Appendix B.

4 Retrieval Effectiveness

We first evaluate whether FLINT’s fixed-budget representations preserve retrieval effectiveness relative to fixed-budget and token-level late-interaction baselines. Storage and retrieval-time efficiency are explored separately in Section 5.

4.1 Overall Retrieval Effectiveness

Table 1 reports NDCG@10 on BEIR and the three complex-query benchmarks; additional Recall@1000 results are reported separately in Appendix Table 6. FLINT remains competitive with ConstBERT on BEIR, showing that symmetric attention-based pooling preserves effectiveness on conventional, predominantly short-query retrieval tasks. For example, on Quora, FLINT achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.848, outperforming ConstBERT at 0.817 and closely approaching ColBERTv2 at 0.855. ColBERTv2 nevertheless performs better on many BEIR collections and has the highest BERT-based average, which illustrates the effectiveness advantage that full token-level representations can retain in the short-query domain.

FLINT’s advantage becomes clearer on the complex-query benchmarks. Among the BERT-based models, FLINT achieves the highest average NDCG@10 on CRUMB, TREC-ToT 2025, and BrowseComp+. For example, on TREC-ToT 2025, FLINT improves NDCG@10 from 0.047 with ConstBERT to 0.065 and also exceeds ColBERTv2 at 0.046. Although the absolute scores on these benchmarks are lower than on BEIR, this reflects the substantially greater difficulty of the tasks, which involve long, out-of-distribution queries, limited lexical overlap, uncertain recollections, and challenging distractor documents.

Overall, FLINT preserves competitive effectiveness on conventional retrieval tasks while providing stronger ranking effectiveness on longer and more complex information needs. Although token-level ColBERTv2 remains more effective on some datasets, FLINT’s ability to retain competitive effectiveness with compact representations is valuable in light of the substantial storage and latency reductions examined in Section 5.

4.2 Impact of the Backbone Encoder

We next examine how the backbone encoder affects FLINT’s retrieval effectiveness.

As shown in Table 1, replacing BERT with ModernBERT consistently improves FLINT across all benchmark suites. Average NDCG@10 increases from 0.452 to 0.530 on BEIR and from 0.145 to 0.205 on CRUMB. The gains are particularly pronounced on the complex-query benchmarks. FLINT improves from 0.065 to 0.147 on TREC-ToT 2025 and from 0.063 to 0.105 on BrowseComp+. These results show that FLINT benefits substantially from a stronger backbone, especially on longer and out-of-distribution information needs.

With the backbone and training held fixed, FLINT outperforms ConstBERT on every suite on ModernBERT. The gap is largest on TREC-ToT 2025, whose queries are the longest and most conversational, where ConstBERT reaches less than half of FLINT’s score. Compared with ModernBERT ColBERTv2, FLINT is nearly tied on BEIR (0.530 vs. 0.534) and outperforms it on CRUMB (0.205 vs. 0.184). ModernBERT ColBERTv2 remains ahead on TREC-ToT 2025 and BrowseComp+. FLINT is stronger than the single-vector baseline, particularly on long queries, where NDCG@10 rises from 0.042 to 0.147 on TREC-ToT 2025 and from 0.022 to 0.105 on BrowseComp+. This indicates that retaining multiple pooled vectors, rather than pooling to a single vector, is central to its effectiveness.

4.3 Impact of the Budget VV

We examine how the number of vectors per query and document, VV, affects FLINT’s effectiveness with the ModernBERT backbone. Reducing the budget from V=32V{=}32 to V=16V{=}16 lowers effectiveness across all benchmark suites. Nevertheless, FLINT with V=16V{=}16 still outperforms the single-vector baseline on every suite and ModernBERT ConstBERT on all three complex-query suites, while requiring approximately half of ConstBERT’s index size.

Increasing the budget from V=32V{=}32 to V=64V{=}64 leaves average BEIR effectiveness nearly unchanged (0.531 vs. 0.530) but improves performance on complex queries. These results suggest that longer, multi-constraint queries benefit from a larger vector budget, whereas the predominantly short queries in BEIR gain little beyond V=32V{=}32. The budget thus provides a direct way to trade additional storage and computation for improved effectiveness on complex queries.

5 Efficiency Analysis

We next evaluate FLINT’s storage and retrieval-time efficiency relative to baselines on NFCorpus, CRUMB Paper, CRUMB Clinical, and TREC-ToT 2025. We select these corpora to examine how efficiency varies with both corpus size and query length. They span 3.6K to 6.4M documents and mean query lengths of 7 to 204 tokens. The indexing and timing setup is described in Appendix B.

5.1 Retrieval Latency

Table 2 reports retrieval mean response time (MRT), decomposed into query-encoding and search time, for both BERT and ModernBERT backbones. Here, unless otherwise stated, FLINT uses V=32V{=}32. On the three long-query corpora, FLINT achieves 1.61.6–2.8×2.8\times faster retrieval than ConstBERT with BERT and 1.51.5–2.7×2.7\times with ModernBERT. The largest gains occur on TREC-ToT 2025, where MRT falls from 74.3 to 26.1 ms with BERT and from 140.9 to 51.3 ms with ModernBERT. Relative to ColBERTv2, FLINT is 10.510.5–36.2×36.2\times faster with BERT and 2323–170×170\times faster with ModernBERT on these corpora. On NFCorpus, whose queries average only seven tokens, FLINT and ConstBERT have very similar MRT. FLINT’s latency advantage over the late-interaction baselines is strongest on long queries.

Figure 3 illustrates where these latency gains arise, whether from query encoding or search. As shown in the figure, FLINT and ConstBERT differ in how their MRT is distributed between encoding and search. With the same backbone, FLINT and ConstBERT have similar query-encoding costs. Their search times, however, diverge sharply as search time accounts for most of ConstBERT’s MRT on the long-query corpora. For example, FLINT searches 2.52.5–4.6×4.6\times faster with BERT and 2.52.5–4.8×4.8\times faster with ModernBERT. FLINT’s lower MRT comes primarily from faster search, while its query-encoding time remains similar to that of the baselines.

The ModernBERT rows of Table 2 extend this comparison to the single-vector baseline and FLINT with V∈{16,32,64}V\in\{16,32,64\}. Single-Vector is the fastest ModernBERT system, since its search takes about 1 ms, but it is far less effective (Section 4.2).

Section 4.3 showed how the budget VV affects effectiveness; here, we report its latency cost. Compared with the single-vector baseline, FLINT with V=16V{=}16 adds 6–16 ms of MRT while improving effectiveness across all benchmarks. Increasing VV further raises search cost. For example, V=16V{=}16 searches in at most 12.1 ms and V=32V{=}32 in at most 23.6 ms, whereas V=64V{=}64 takes 31.4–75.1 ms on the long-query corpora, 2.82.8–4.9×4.9\times the search time of V=32V{=}32. FLINT’s budget provides a controllable trade-off between effectiveness and latency, with the additional effectiveness gains from larger budgets coming at higher search cost.

5.2 Latency Scaling with Query Length

FLINT’s latency advantage increases with query length because it always produces a constant number of VV (here VV=32) query vectors and thus its search cost remains nearly constant, whereas ConstBERT retains one representation per query token and therefore becomes increasingly expensive on longer queries. As shown in Figure 4, on TREC-ToT 2025 with BERT, the encoding time for longer queries increases at the same rate for both FLINT and ConstBERT models (left). However, their search times diverge sharply (middle). FLINT’s search time remains nearly constant relative to number of vectors in the query, with a fitted slope of 0.0040.004 ms per token, compared with 0.310.31 ms for ConstBERT. Consequently, FLINT’s total MRT grows only slightly with query length, while ConstBERT’s increases much more steeply (right). The same pattern holds with ModernBERT. Truncating ConstBERT’s queries to 32 tokens would also cap its query-vector count, but reduces average NDCG@10 on every complex-query suite with both backbones (Appendix F).

5.3 PLAID Cell Activation

PLAID does not score every document in the corpus. Each query vector probes its nearest centroids, activating the corresponding cells and contributing documents to the candidate pool. The union of the corresponding cells determines the candidate documents that are then scored with MaxSim. Therefore, activating more cells broadens the search and generally increases the number of candidates; activating fewer cells reduces search work. However, fewer activated cells are useful only insofar as the resulting candidate pool is still effective. Figure 5 shows that FLINT consistently activates fewer cells than ConstBERT on the three long-query corpora. This translates into fewer candidate documents, as ConstBERT scores 2.32.3–4.6×4.6\times more candidates across the two backbones. It also compares each candidate against 55–7×7\times more query vectors. FLINT therefore reduces search work by scoring fewer candidates and performing fewer vector comparisons per candidate.

The reduction in activated cells is larger on BERT, where FLINT’s pooled vectors are also more concentrated in direction and probe fewer distinct cells (Appendix D). These savings accompany competitive effectiveness relative to ConstBERT on conventional retrieval and stronger results on the complex-query suites, showing that FLINT can search a smaller candidate pool without sacrificing overall retrieval effectiveness.

5.4 Index Size

Table 3 reports on-disk index sizes. Because FLINT and ConstBERT both store 32 vectors per document, their BERT indices are nearly identical, so FLINT’s latency reductions do not come at the cost of a larger index. The same holds on ModernBERT. Compared with token-level ColBERTv2, FLINT’s indices are 5.35.3–5.8×5.8\times smaller with BERT and 6.86.8–9.3×9.3\times smaller with ModernBERT.

The fixed document-vector budget makes storage per document independent of document length, with index size scaling with VV instead. This provides direct control over storage requirements. Single-vector retrieval yields even smaller indices on the three larger corpora, but at a substantial cost in effectiveness (Section 4). These results show that FLINT’s fixed document-vector budget prevents the index from growing with document length. Combined with the response-time results above, FLINT provides the storage efficiency of ConstBERT while achieving markedly lower latency than both ConstBERT and token-level retrieval on the larger, long-query corpora.

6 Conclusion

We introduced FLINT, a fixed-budget late-interaction architecture that addresses two central scaling challenges: document storage and query-side search cost. Shared attention-based pooling maps both queries and documents to a fixed number of vectors, preserving multi-vector matching without retaining one vector per token.

FLINT achieves 5.35.3–9.3×9.3\times smaller indices than token-level models and, on the long-query corpora, 1.51.5–2.8×2.8\times faster end-to-end retrieval than ConstBERT. Its search latency remains nearly constant as queries grow longer. With the vector budget VV controlling the effectiveness–efficiency trade-off, FLINT makes storage and search computation explicit architectural choices, supporting efficient retrieval for long and complex queries.

Limitations

Training distribution.

Our BERT FLINT model is supervised on the same MS MARCO passage triples as ColBERTv2 and ConstBERT. We adopt this deliberately, so that differences between FLINT, ConstBERT, and ColBERTv2 reflect the pooling architecture rather than the training data, but it means the only query distribution the pooling module ever observes during training is MS MARCO’s short, keyword-like queries. Our central claims concern long, complex queries, so those results are entirely zero-shot generalization. To our knowledge, there is no comparable MS MARCO-scale dataset of high-quality long queries. Moreover, multi-vector retrievers are known to be sensitive to both the scale and quality of training data. We therefore leave long-query-specific training to future work.

Limited budget sweep.

On BERT we fix the budget at V=32V{=}32, matching ConstBERT’s setting so the two fixed-budget systems are directly comparable. We vary V∈{16,32,64}V\in\{16,32,64\} only on ModernBERT, so it remains open whether symmetric pooling degrades more or less gracefully than document-only pooling at smaller budgets, and whether a larger budget would close FLINT’s remaining gap to ColBERTv2 on BEIR. We also tie the query and document budgets to the same value. Decoupling them, for instance a smaller query budget paired with a larger document budget, is unexplored.

Scope of the evaluation.

On BERT, absolute effectiveness on the complex-query suites is low for every system we evaluate, with the best NDCG@10 on TREC Tip-of-the-Tongue 2025 reaching only 0.0650.065. FLINT’s improvements in this regime are consistent across suites, but they are improvements within a band where all late-interaction models we test perform poorly, and the small absolute margins should be read with that in mind. Our evaluation also covers two encoder-only backbones of modest scale, so behavior under substantially larger backbones remains untested.

GenAI Usage Disclosure

We used large language models to edit the grammar and wording of this paper, to assist with coding, and to help clean up the code repository for release. The research design, analysis, interpretation of results, and conclusions are entirely our own.

Appendix A Related Work

Fixed-size multi-vector representations.

MetaEmbed (Xiao et al., 2026) appends learnable tokens to the input of a vision-language model and uses their final hidden states as multi-vector embeddings for multimodal retrieval, trained with Matryoshka-style nested groups so the number of vectors can be chosen at test time. FLINT instead targets long-query text retrieval and pools the encoder outputs with a separate cross-attention module rather than adding tokens to the input. It uses a fixed budget VV per model instead of nested groups, and projects each vector to a low dimension, whereas MetaEmbed keeps the full hidden dimension, creating much larger indices. They also focus primarily on multi-modal benchmarks rather than on long and complex textual datasets.

Poly-encoders (Humeau et al., 2020) use learned codes that attend over the query tokens to produce several query vectors, while each document remains a single vector compared through attention. FLINT pools both queries and documents into multiple vectors and scores them with MaxSim.

ConstBERT (MacAvaney et al., 2025) pools each document into a fixed number of vectors with a learned linear layer and keeps queries token-level without compression. FLINT pools both sides with cross-attention, so query cost does not grow with query length.

Reducing token vectors.

Token pooling (Clavié et al., 2024) clusters document token vectors post-hoc, and static pruning (Acquavia et al., 2023) removes low-impact document vectors. As presented in both papers, however, the number of vectors still grows with document length and queries are unchanged, whereas FLINT learns a fixed number of vectors for both sides.

Query embedding pruning (Tonellotto and Macdonald, 2021) keeps the query token vectors of the rarest terms for candidate generation. FLINT instead learns to summarize all query tokens into VV vectors and also fixes the document side vector count.

Efficient multi-vector search.

XTR (Lee et al., 2023) trains the model so that its first-stage token retrieval finds the relevant document tokens, then scores documents using only those retrieved tokens. This skips loading every candidate’s full set of vectors, but it keeps one vector per token for queries and documents, so its index is as large as ColBERT’s. WARP (Scheerer et al., 2025) is a faster search engine for XTR-style retrieval, but its index still stores one vector per token. MUVERA (Dhulipala et al., 2024) is a latency-focused prefilter: it compresses each multi-vector set into one fixed-dimensional encoding (FDE) for fast single-vector candidate search, then reranks candidates with the full token-level vectors. Because the FDE index sits on top of the full multi-vector index, its storage exceeds that of the multi-vector index alone, whereas FLINT reduces storage.

Single-vector retrieval.

With V=32V{=}32 vectors of dimension 128, FLINT represents each input with 4096 values. Single-vector models that produce vector embeddings with the same amount of floats, such as RepLLaMA (Ma et al., 2024), rely on much larger backbones: it fine-tunes LLaMA-7B as a bi-encoder producing one 4096-dimensional vector scored by dot product. To our knowledge, no single-vector model with a similarly sized and performing backbone produces embeddings of this size. A size-matched comparison would thus alter the backbone’s strength, and we therefore leave it out of scope. We instead compare against a single-vector model with the same backbone and training data (Section 4.2).

Other approaches.

TRIAL (Kang et al., 2025) improves the scoring function rather than compressing representations; SCV (Park et al., 2025) compresses only documents via span pooling with a single-vector prefilter, so query-side cost still scales with query length; Zong & Piwowarski (Zong and Piwowarski, 2025) dynamically prune document tokens, with pruning ratio varying per document and query tokens left uncompressed. FLINT compresses queries and documents to a fixed, input-length-independent budget.

Appendix B Experimental Settings

Training. On BERT, FLINT is trained on MS MARCO passage-ranking triples with 64 candidates per query, in fp16 with a global batch size of 48, a learning rate of 10−510^{-5}, and a linear schedule over 267K steps. On ModernBERT-large, we train the FLINT (V∈{16,32,64}V\in\{16,32,64\}), ConstBERT (3232 document vectors), and ColBERTv2 architectures ourselves (ModernBERT FLINT, ModernBERT ConstBERT, and ModernBERT ColBERTv2) under the multi-vector training regimen of Warner et al. (2025), on MS MARCO with 32 candidates per query, for one epoch in bf16 with a global batch size of 16, a learning rate of 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}, and 5% warmup. The FLINT pooling module uses a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}. Training queries are truncated to 84 tokens. The single-vector baseline is a publicly available ModernBERT-large bi-encoder,33 3 https://huggingface.co/joe32140/ModernBERT-large-msmarco trained identically to the single-vector retriever introduced in (Warner et al., 2025).

Pooling module. The pooling module uses H=8H{=}8 attention heads and a feed-forward expansion ratio of r=4r{=}4 on BERT (h=768h{=}768) and r=2r{=}2 on ModernBERT (h=1024h{=}1024), with dropout 0.1. Pooled vectors are projected to h′=128h^{\prime}{=}128 dimensions. On BERT, the query and document sides use separate projections; on ModernBERT, they share one.

Sequence lengths. At evaluation, queries are truncated to M=512M{=}512 tokens for every model. The evaluation document length NN differs between backbones because of ConstBERT: its learned pooling maps a fixed number of token positions to its 32 document vectors, so NN is fixed when ConstBERT is trained. The released BERT ConstBERT checkpoint uses N=250N{=}250, so we truncate documents to N=250N{=}250 for all BERT models. On ModernBERT, we train ConstBERT with N=512N{=}512 and truncate documents to N=512N{=}512 for all ModernBERT models. Within each backbone, every model therefore sees the same document context.

Query padding. BERT ConstBERT and ColBERTv2 pad queries shorter than 32 tokens up to 32, matching ColBERTv2’s default and the setting they were trained with. All ModernBERT models are trained without query padding and are evaluated the same way. BERT FLINT queries are not padded during training or evaluation, and FLINT always produces VV query vectors.

Indexing and retrieval. Multi-vector models are indexed with PLAID (Santhanam et al., 2022a; MacAvaney and Tonellotto, 2024) using 2-bit residual compression. For the efficiency results, every multi-vector model uses PLAID with ncells=8=8 and k=1000k=1000 retrieved candidates, and the single-vector model uses a FAISS OPQ-IVFPQ index (Jégou et al., 2011).

Latency measurement. All latency experiments run on a single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU. All systems for a corpus are timed on the same machine. After a global warm-up, we take the median of three timed runs per query. Query-encoding time covers the model forward pass, and search time covers candidate retrieval and scoring.

Appendix C Dataset Details

Table 8 provides detailed statistics for the four evaluation suites, including corpus and query counts, mean document and query lengths, task focus, and query characteristics. Lengths are measured using the ColBERT tokenizer. For suites containing multiple corpora or tasks, we report the range across the evaluated collections. We exclude CRUMB Legal and SetOps from our tables since queries are short (148 and 47 characters, respectively vs. 415 for Theorem, the next shortest). They did not fit in our curation of long query benchmarks. We report their results, along with MS MARCO, in Table 4.

Appendix D Query Geometry and Effective Rank

Section 5.3 shows that FLINT activates fewer PLAID cells than ConstBERT. Beyond the number of query vectors, the cells a query activates also depend on how spread out its vectors are: vectors pointing in similar directions tend to probe the same centroids. We quantify this spread using effective rank, or the participation ratio (Gao et al., 2017):

erank⁡(Q)=(∑iλi)2∑iλi2,λi=σi2​(Q),\mathrm{erank}(Q)=\frac{\left(\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\right)^{2}}{\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}^{2}},\qquad\lambda_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}(Q), (3)

where lower effective rank indicates that the query vectors are concentrated along fewer directions.

Spread of the query vectors. Figure 6 divides ConstBERT’s participation ratio by FLINT’s at each query length. On BERT, the two are nearly equal on the shortest queries (0.960.96–1.011.01 at 8 tokens), and ConstBERT’s ratio grows faster as queries get longer, reaching 1.78×1.78\times FLINT’s on CRUMB Clinical, 1.45×1.45\times on CRUMB Paper, and 1.26×1.26\times on TREC-ToT 2025. FLINT’s pooled vectors therefore stay more concentrated than ConstBERT’s token vectors. On ModernBERT, the ratio stays between 0.870.87 and 1.191.19 at every length, so the two models’ query vectors are about equally spread out.

Spread and cell activation on BERT. Figure 7 connects this spread to PLAID search on BERT. Across 3,2483{,}248 queries, the participation ratio is strongly associated with the number of activated cells (ρ=0.87\rho=0.87), and cell activation closely tracks the number of candidate documents scored (within-corpus r=0.99r=0.99). The participation ratio also correlates with PLAID-search latency on CRUMB Paper (ρ=0.84\rho=0.84, n=1,008n=1{,}008), although this pooled correlation also reflects ConstBERT’s query length.

Cells at the same number of query vectors. Both the number of query vectors and their spread affect how many cells a query activates. To separate the two, we give ConstBERT the same number of vectors as FLINT by randomly sampling 32 of its token vectors per query (Figure 8). On BERT, FLINT’s 32 vectors still activate fewer cells than ConstBERT’s 32 (120 vs. 174 on CRUMB Paper, 138 vs. 190 on CRUMB Clinical), which matches their lower spread. On ModernBERT, the two activate the same number of cells (167 vs. 163 and 174 vs. 177), which matches their equal spread. With all of its token vectors, ConstBERT activates 2.32.3–4.1×4.1\times more cells than FLINT on both backbones. Most of FLINT’s reduction in activated cells therefore comes from using fewer query vectors, and on BERT the lower spread of its pooled vectors adds to it.

Pooling variants. Table 5 reports mean query and document effective ranks for ColBERTv2, ConstBERT, and FLINT-symmetric, and for BERT-FLINT architecture variants. Primary FLINT-symmetric shares the perceiver across both sides; unless marked query-side, the variant block changes only the document-side pooler. Deep and iterative-shallow doc-side variants sit near erank≈1\mathrm{erank}\!\approx\!1, indicating near-total directional collapse of the latent set, whereas no-SA and the query-side perceiver retain higher ranks closer to ConstBERT and ColBERTv2. FLINT-symmetric sits below ConstBERT on query rank, consistent with the BERT results above.

Appendix E Recall Statistics for Complex Query Benchmarks

Table 6 reports Recall@1000 on the three complex-query suites, complementing the NDCG@10 results of Table 1. With the BERT backbone, FLINT recalls more than ConstBERT on Clinical (0.3510.351 vs. 0.3060.306) and TREC-ToT (0.3230.323 vs. 0.2770.277), while ConstBERT recalls more on Paper (0.4430.443 vs. 0.4000.400) and Theorem (0.3820.382 vs. 0.2460.246); the two models are close on CRUMB overall (0.3720.372 vs. 0.3950.395) and on BrowseComp+ (0.3910.391 vs. 0.4010.401). With ModernBERT, FLINT (V=32V{=}32) recalls more than ConstBERT on every collection, with the largest gaps on TREC-ToT (0.4580.458 vs. 0.2720.272) and BrowseComp+ (0.5550.555 vs. 0.4660.466). It also recalls more than ModernBERT ColBERTv2 on every collection except CRUMB ToT (0.5260.526 vs. 0.5780.578), including CRUMB overall (0.5080.508 vs. 0.4410.441), TREC-ToT (0.4580.458 vs. 0.4020.402), and BrowseComp+ (0.5550.555 vs. 0.5260.526). Raising the budget to V=64V{=}64 further improves recall (CRUMB 0.5250.525, BrowseComp+ 0.5760.576), while the single-vector model trails every FLINT variant on CRUMB and BrowseComp+.

Appendix F Query Truncation for ConstBERT

Table 7 reports ConstBERT’s effectiveness when its queries are truncated to 32 tokens, which gives it at most as many query vectors as FLINT. Truncation lowers average NDCG@10 on CRUMB from 0.1360.136 to 0.0950.095, on TREC-ToT 2025 from 0.0470.047 to 0.0180.018, and on BrowseComp+ from 0.0550.055 to 0.0370.037. StackExchange is the only collection where it helps (0.1700.170 vs. 0.1400.140). ModernBERT ConstBERT shows the same pattern: truncation lowers average NDCG@10 from 0.1800.180 to 0.1270.127 on CRUMB, from 0.0700.070 to 0.0320.032 on TREC-ToT 2025, and from 0.0670.067 to 0.0360.036 on BrowseComp+, and StackExchange is essentially unchanged (0.2090.209 vs. 0.2070.207). Truncating the query is therefore very lossy on both backbones, and it does not substitute for learned compression of the query into a fixed budget.
